headline: Highest risk is medium prompt-injection and data-leakage via shared files/MCP and broad egress; no evidence of critical harm, but defaults are not isolated.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LightAgent can use MCP, browsers, stdin/stdout, and broad egress, so it can ingest attacker-controlled content; marketingskills explicitly uses shared skill files and shared context. That creates a plausible instruction-hijack path if LightAgent outputs are fed into the marketing skill chain. The pairwise bridge is documented only indirectly, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF LightAgent outputs are copied into marketingskills skill files or shared context, injection becomes actionable.
IF either agent treats file or browser content as trusted instructions, attacker text can steer downstream behavior.
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces.
Disable automatic ingestion of browser/file content into prompts.
Add a provenance tag to all cross-agent text.
Review any shared skill files before reuse.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation.

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightAgent touches user conversations, long-term memory, tool results, and provenance metadata, while marketingskills reads and writes skill/context files. If they share a workspace or the same files, sensitive context can flow from A into B and then into outputs. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace by default, so this is medium rather than high.
conditions: IF both agents mount the same directory, B can read A's artifacts.
IF LightAgent persists memory or traces to files, marketingskills can ingest them.
mitigations: Use separate directories for each agent.
Restrict B to a read-only copy of any shared inputs.
Delete or redact traces before handoff.
Audit file permissions on .agents and .claude paths.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LightAgent has spawn_subprocesses and broad network egress; marketingskills has read/write filesystem plus subprocesses. If they operate on the same mutable files or shared context, concurrent writes can conflict and corrupt state. The profiles do not show locking or coordination, so the overlap is real but not proven dangerous enough for high.
conditions: IF both agents write the same workspace, file races can occur.
IF either agent modifies shared skill files without locks, state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output paths.
Serialize writes with a simple operator-run lock file.
Run one agent at a time for shared resources.
Back up shared files before edits.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightAgent can generate tool results and workflow state that marketingskills may reuse as shared context. marketingskills' skill-based workflow suggests it may build on prior context, so unverified outputs from A can cascade into B's marketing content. Because B is not documented as blindly authoritative, medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF B consumes A's generated text without verification, errors propagate.
IF A's tool results are copied into marketing drafts, factual mistakes can be amplified.
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents.
Mark A outputs as untrusted input.
Cross-check claims against source documents.
Keep citations attached through the handoff.
requires-engineering: add validation gates before B can act on A outputs.

E_compliance.rationale: LightAgent handles secrets and long-term memory, while marketingskills is a marketing skill package with file-based context and no stated regulated-data handling. There is no explicit residency or certification mismatch in the profiles, so compliance risk is limited to accidental over-sharing rather than a documented breach path. I cite both because the concern is the handoff of sensitive data into B's files.
conditions: IF regulated or secret data is placed into B's skill files, retention and access controls may be violated.
IF A's memory contains personal data and B persists it in marketing artifacts, deletion/export handling becomes harder.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of marketing files.
Redact secrets before handoff.
Set a short retention window for shared artifacts.
Document which data classes may cross the boundary.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention.
